title: Open, Save, Quit
subtitle: Start here: choose an editor, open a file, make a change, save it, and get out
summary: Start from nothing. Install Neovim or enable Vim controls in your current editor, then open a file, type, move, select, delete, copy, save, and quit.

blocks.text: Open, Save, Quit

Start here. This section assumes that you have never opened Vim and do not know what its modes are. You do not need a configuration, a plugin manager, or a new terminal. By the end, you will be able to do enough ordinary editing to leave Vim controls turned on all day. You will be slow. That is fine. Speed comes later.
Choose where to use Vim

The simplest standalone route is a terminal and **Neovim**, the modern editor used throughout this book. But learning Vim does not require abandoning the editor you already know. VS Code, Visual Studio, and JetBrains IDEs all have good Vim emulators. Start where you already work; the editing language travels with you.

rows: Try `vi --version` or `vim --version` first; one is commonly already installed. Otherwise install [Neovim](https://neovim.io/doc/install/) with your package manager.
Try `vi --version` first; macOS includes a `vi`-compatible editor. For modern Neovim, install [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) and run `brew install neovim`.
Windows itself does not normally include Vim. Run `winget install Neovim.Neovim`, or install [WSL](https://learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl/install) and use the Linux editor inside it.
Use the [Vim downloads page](https://www.vim.org/download.php). Vim is completely suitable for everything in this book.

[VSCodeVim](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=vscodevim.vim) for easy setup; [VSCode Neovim](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=asvetliakov.vscode-neovim) to use real Neovim as the editing engine
[VsVim](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=JaredParMSFT.VsVim), a mature Vim emulator whose core is written in F#

blocks.text: Already productive in another editor? Keep it. Install its Vim extension and learn the keys in familiar surroundings. You can move to Neovim later — or never.

In VS Code, open the Extensions view, search for `VSCodeVim`, and select **Install**. In Visual Studio, open **Extensions → Manage Extensions** and search for `VsVim`. In a JetBrains IDE, open **Settings → Plugins**, search for `IdeaVim`, and select **Install**. Restart the editor if it asks. Then open any disposable text file and continue with "Your first edit" below.
What may already be installed

Do not install anything until you check. Run `nvim --version`, `vim --version`, and `vi --version`, in that order. If one prints a version banner, you already have an editor with which to begin. Full Linux installations and Linux distributions under WSL commonly include `vi` or Vim; minimal containers may not. macOS includes a `vi`-compatible editor. Native Windows normally requires Neovim, Vim, WSL, or an editor extension.

If only `vi` is available, use it for this first session. Install Neovim when convenient. On macOS with Homebrew, run `brew install neovim`. On Windows, run `winget install Neovim.Neovim`. On Ubuntu, Debian, or Ubuntu under WSL, run `sudo apt install neovim`. Other distributions use their normal package managers. The [official Neovim installation page](https://neovim.io/doc/install/) has current commands and direct downloads.
Opening a file

Open a terminal, move to a directory in which you can create a file, and run `nvim hello.txt`. If you are using Vim or the built-in Unix editor, use `vim hello.txt` or `vi hello.txt` instead. If the file exists, you see its contents. If it does not, you see an empty buffer that *will* be saved as `hello.txt` the first time you write. Vim does not create the file on disk until you save.
Your first edit

Vim opens in *normal mode,* where letter keys issue commands instead of inserting text. Press {key:i} once to enter *insert mode.* Type `Hello from Vim!` just as you would in any editor. Then press {key:Esc} to return to *normal mode.*

Now try the four movement keys: {key:h} moves left, {key:j} moves down, {key:k} moves up, and {key:l} moves right. Arrow keys work too. For this first minute, use whichever keys let you stay oriented.

If typing letters moves the cursor or changes text unexpectedly, press {key:Esc} once. You are back in *normal mode.* Press {key:i} whenever you want to type more text. That small loop — {key:i}, type, {key:Esc} — is enough to begin.
Save and return to the shell

Press {key:Esc} to make sure you are in *normal mode.* Type `:wq`, then press {key:Enter}. The colon opens Vim's command line, `w` writes the file, and `q` quits the editor. Back at the shell, run `cat hello.txt` to confirm that your line reached the disk.
That was a complete Vim session. Everything below gives you separate commands for saving, quitting, and recovering when Vim refuses to exit.
The Minimum for Your First Day

You do not have to learn the whole keyboard before using Vim for real work. For your first day, remember one loop: press {key:i} to type, press {key:Esc} when you finish typing, move somewhere else, and press {key:i} again. Save with `:w`. Leave with `:x`. If anything feels wrong, press {key:Esc} and begin the loop again.

rows: Use the arrow keys, or begin trying {key:h}, {key:j}, {key:k}, and {key:l}.

blocks.text: Arrow Keys Are Allowed

The arrow keys work in Vim. Use them while you are learning. Reaching for them is slower than keeping your hand on {key:hjkl}, but being temporarily slow is better than being lost. Begin substituting {key:h}, {key:j}, {key:k}, and {key:l} when you remember. Do not disable the arrows or punish yourself for using them. The home-row motions will take over naturally as the rest of the grammar becomes familiar.
Select First, Act Second -- for Now

If you are used to selecting text before cutting or copying it, Vim lets you work that way. Press {key:Esc} to enter *normal mode,* move to the start of some text, and press {key:v} to enter *visual mode.* Move with the arrows or {key:hjkl}; Vim highlights the selection. Then press {key:d} to delete it, which also saves it for pasting, or press {key:y} to copy it without deleting it. Press {key:p} to put the saved text after the cursor. Press {key:u} if the result is wrong.

Selection-first editing is a bridge, not a mistake. Later you will usually skip the selection and describe the edit directly: {key:d}{key:w} deletes a word, {key:y}{key:y} copies a line, and {key:c}{key:i}{key:w} changes the word under the cursor. For now, {key:v}, move, then {key:d} or {key:y} is perfectly good Vim.
The First-Week Bargain

If your work allows it, leave Vim controls enabled for ordinary editing this week. Keep the arrow keys. Keep using the mouse when you need it. Keep a familiar editor around for emergencies. The only commitment is to perform routine edits with the small set above instead of turning Vim off whenever you slow down.

Expect to be slower for weeks and uneven for months. Vim becomes fast by replacing conscious key recall with muscle memory, and muscle memory cannot be rushed. The immediate goal is not speed. It is reaching the point at which you can finish a normal day without escaping back to a different editing model.
Saving

blocks.label: Write the buffer to its file

blocks.text: `:w` "writes" — Vim's word for save. `:w` {filename} writes to a different filename (Save As). `:w!` forces a write through read-only flags.
Quitting
`:q` quits — *if* the buffer is clean. If there are unsaved changes, Vim refuses and tells you to save or force-quit. Force-quit with `:q!` discards changes and exits.
Save and quit

rows: Write, then quit. Always writes (even if nothing changed).
Write *if changed,* then quit. Quieter than `:wq`.
Same as `:x` — write-if-changed, then quit. Normal-mode shortcut.

blocks.text: Use {key:Z}{key:Z} as your default "done" key — no colon, no {key:Enter}, just two capital Zs. It's also the most ergonomic of the bunch.
Quit without saving

If you ever quit with `:q!` and regret it, remember: Vim writes a per-session swapfile. The next time you open the file, Vim may offer to recover. The undo *file* (if you have `undofile` set) survives quit, so you can even reopen and undo back to a state before the changes you discarded.
Reference

blocks.title: Buffers, Files, and What `:w` Actually Does
blocks.text:
When you open a file, Vim copies it into memory as a *buffer* — an in-memory list of lines. Your edits change the buffer, not the file. `:w` (write) flushes the buffer to disk; until then, the on-disk file is unchanged.

Vim also creates a *swapfile* (`.<filename>.swp`) next to the buffer's file. The swapfile is a periodic snapshot of unsaved changes; if Vim or your machine crashes, the swapfile lets the next `nvim <file>` invocation recover. This is also what causes the "swap file already exists" prompt — usually Vim was killed without exiting cleanly, and the swap is still on disk.

The *undofile* (separate from the swap, controlled by `undofile`) persists the undo *tree* across sessions: open a file tomorrow and {key:u} can still walk back through today's edits.

Quitting with {key:Z}{key:Z} (or `:x`) writes the buffer if it's modified and exits. Quitting with {key:Z}{key:Q} (or `:q!`) deletes the swapfile and exits without writing — your unsaved buffer changes are gone, but the on-disk file is intact (it never got written this session).

blocks.title: Multiple Files
blocks.text:
Vim can hold many buffers at once. `:e` {file} opens *another* file in a new buffer, leaving the previous one in memory. `:ls` lists all loaded buffers. `:b` {n} switches to buffer N.

This matters for quitting: `:q` closes the current *window;* if other windows or buffers are open, Vim is still running. `:qa` (quit-all) closes everything. `:wqa` writes-all-then-quits-all. If you've ever pressed `:q` expecting Vim to exit and gotten "E37: No write since last change" or seen it switch to another buffer instead — it's because the buffer/window distinction matters even at this level.

Full treatment in `windows.buffers`.

blocks.title: Why It's Spelled `:w`, `:q`, `:wq`
blocks.text:
The colon-prefixed commands are not Vim's invention. They are *ex* commands — Bill Joy's line editor from 1976 — that `vi` inherited and that Vim/Neovim still implement faithfully. Ex itself was an extension of *ed,* Ken Thompson's 1969 line editor.

In ex, you addressed lines with line numbers and ran commands on them: `1,$s/foo/bar/g` ("on lines 1 to last, substitute foo with bar globally"). The single-letter command names — `w` for write, `q` for quit, `s` for substitute, `d` for delete, `y` for yank — were chosen for terseness, because users were typing on slow serial lines where every character cost real time.

This is why colon commands feel like a different language inside Vim: they *are* a different language, descended from a different lineage. The {key::} keystroke is a gear-shift. To the left of the colon you are speaking visual-mode `vi`; to the right, you are speaking ex. Both languages compose: `:w` writes, `:5,10w` writes lines 5–10 to a file, `:%s/foo/bar/g` runs an ex substitution on the whole buffer.

blocks.title: Buffers carry a dirty bit
blocks.text: Saving and quitting aren't symmetric. The buffer carries a `modified` flag that flips on the first edit and clears on a successful write. `:q` consults that flag and refuses to exit (E37) unless you force it with {key:!}; `:x` is a conditional `write-then-quit` that skips the write when the flag is already clear. {key:Z}{key:Z} is the same conditional path as `:x`; {key:Z}{key:Q} is the unconditional discard path of `:q!`. Internally these are four code paths, not four shortcuts.
